settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: engineVerify (lines 111-126) and engineSign (lines 173-187) do enforce a minimum length of getDigestLength() whenever HMACOutputLengthSet is true, so a small value is normally rejected with XMLSignatureException("algorithms.HMACOutputLengthMin").
reset() (lines 97-101) clears both the length value and the set flag, which reduces the chance of stale state carrying an attacker value across operations.
engineInitVerify (lines 135-164) requires a SecretKey and initializes the Mac before verification, so verification is bound to a real key.
candidates.description:
IntegrityHmac (used by IntegrityHmacSHA1/SHA2-style subclasses backing the ds:HMACSignature algorithms) handles the optional ds:HMACOutputLength element that an attacker can place inside the ds:SignatureMethod element of a signature being verified.

Root cause and data flow:
- engineGetContextFromElement(Element) (lines 325-339) reads the HMACOutputLength text node from the signature DOM (XMLUtils.selectDsNodeText(..., Constants._TAG_HMACOUTPUTLENGTH, 0)) and does this.HMACOutputLength = Integer.parseInt(hmaclength.getData()); followed by this.HMACOutputLengthSet = true;. The value is fully attacker-controlled and the parseInt is not wrapped in a try/catch, so a non-numeric length would surface as an unchecked NumberFormatException from deep inside signature processing instead of a controlled XMLSignatureException.
- engineVerify(byte[] signature) (lines 111-126) only enforces the safety rule inside a conditional: if (this.HMACOutputLengthSet && this.HMACOutputLength < getDigestLength()) { throw ... } else { byte[] completeResult = this.macAlgorithm.doFinal(); return MessageDigestAlgorithm.isEqual(completeResult, signature); }. The digest-length floor (getDigestLength(), e.g. 160 for HMAC-SHA1 at lines 388-390) is the defense that prevents an attacker from shortening the HMAC to a few bits to make forgery feasible. That floor is applied only when the HMACOutputLengthSet flag is true.
- engineSign (lines 173-187) and engineSetHMACOutputLength (lines 315-318) show the same flag-driven pattern on the signing side, and reset() (lines 97-101) resets both HMACOutputLength=0 and HMACOutputLengthSet=false.

The security-relevant question is whether the attacker-supplied length always reaches this floor check with HMACOutputLengthSet=true on the verification path, and whether ordering/state reuse (reset between operations) can ever allow verification to proceed with a truncated or attacker-shortened MAC. I did not find source in the allowed spans that forbids a very small (but parseable) length earlier than engineVerify, nor a lower-bound check at parse time in engineGetContextFromElement; the only bound is the getDigestLength() comparison performed at sign/verify time.
missing_evidence: The caller chain from XMLSignature.verify()/SignedInfo into SignatureAlgorithm.engineGetContextFromElement and engineVerify was not traced in original source (outside the allowed spans), so the exact point where HMACOutputLength is parsed relative to verification is unconfirmed.
No test or code was read that demonstrates HMACOutputLengthSet being true/false at verification time, so it is unproven whether a truncated MAC can ever be accepted in practice.
The behavior of Integer.parseInt on non-numeric attacker input (whether it is caught and converted) was not located in surrounding code outside the read spans.
preconditions: Application feeds an attacker-supplied XML signature to this library's HMAC signature verification path (SecureValidation not necessarily enabled).
The attacker controls the ds:SignatureMethod content and can add a ds:HMACOutputLength element (or rely on the default absence of one).
The HMAC secret key used for verification is shared such that an attacker can attempt forgery.
candidates.title: Attacker-controlled HMACOutputLength is parsed without validation and only floor-checked when HMACOutputLengthSet is true

counter_evidence: XMLUtils.createDocumentBuilder(boolean, boolean) (lines 1049-1061) always enables FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, independent of secureValidation, and the default single-arg overload disallows DOCTYPE declarations (lines 1045-1046).
The checks exist and are applied when secure validation is enabled, indicating an intentional opt-in model rather than missing safeguards.
I found no source in the allowed spans that constructs an unguarded DocumentBuilderFactory parsing untrusted input.
candidates.description:
Defensive checks in the DOM signature verification path are conditioned on the secureValidation flag, which callers supply. This documents where protections depend on configuration rather than being unconditional; it is reported to record the guard surface, not as a confirmed flaw.

Observed guards (all executed only when secureValidation is true):
- Reference(Element, String, Manifest, boolean) (lines 231-250) rejects more than MAXIMUM_TRANSFORM_COUNT transforms (lines 241-245).
- getMessageDigestAlgorithm() (lines 261-279) rejects the MD5 digest URI (lines 272-276).

Consequence: when an application calls the library without enabling secure validation, these transform-count and digest-algorithm limits are not applied. Whether that is a vulnerability depends entirely on the host application's configuration, which is outside this repository and was not verified.
missing_evidence: No code or configuration in the read spans was found that sets secureValidation to true by default for the DOM verification API, so the effective default is unconfirmed.
Application-level configuration (e.g. the JSR-105 secure-validation property) is not part of the read spans.
preconditions: Application uses the DOM verification path without setting the secure-validation property/parameter to true.
Attacker supplies a crafted signature (e.g., excessive transforms or an MD5 digest).
candidates.title: Reference digest/transform guards are gated on secureValidation (contextual, not a defect by itself)
